# Interlude — Capacity and the Weakest Link

**Read after Lab 1, before Lab 2** · no Factorio required · ~20 minutes

Lab 1 showed you a gap: two machines whose catalog capacities were 37.5
and 30 workpieces per minute, and a line that delivered 30. Nothing was
broken. Nothing was wasted, either, in any way you could fix by working
harder. This interlude turns that gap into arithmetic you can do for any
line — and into a prediction Lab 2 is built to test.

## Capacity is arithmetic, not aspiration

A machine's **capacity** is the rate it could sustain if material were
always waiting and space always open. In this laboratory it is exact:

$$
\text{craft time} = \frac{\text{recipe seconds}}{\text{machine speed}},
\qquad
\text{capacity} = \frac{60}{\text{craft time}} \text{ per minute.}
$$

The three assembler tiers run at speeds 0.5, 0.75, and 1.25; the
machining recipe takes 2 s of work, inspection and finishing 1 s each.
Every capacity number in this course — 15, 30, 37.5, 45 — comes from
this one division. Real factories need measurement campaigns to learn
these numbers; here you can read them off the nameplate. What you *do*
with them is the same in both worlds.

## The weakest link sets the pace

Put machines in series and their capacities do not add, average, or
negotiate. In a deterministic line, sustained output is:

$$
\text{line capacity} = \min(\text{capacity}_1, \ldots, \text{capacity}_n)
$$

![Installed capacity by stage for a fast → slow → fast line. The line
delivers the minimum; every unit of capacity above the dashed line is
installed but unusable — not through mismanagement, but by
arithmetic.](../images/interludes/line-capacity.svg){width=100%}

The stage achieving that minimum is the **constraint** (you will also
hear *bottleneck*; the flow interlude will call its rate $r_b$). Two
consequences follow immediately, and both are routinely disbelieved by
people meeting them in the wild:

- **Capacity added anywhere but the constraint adds nothing.** Upgrade a
  37.5/min stage to 45 and the min() does not move. The money is spent,
  the output is identical.
- **Installed capacity is not a promise.** Lab 1's line "wasted" 7.5/min
  of the first machine's capability — permanently, structurally, and
  invisibly to anyone auditing the machines one at a time. Only the
  *system* number reveals it.

## "Utilization" needs a denominator

The natural next question — *how busy is each machine?* — is a trap
unless you ask it precisely. "Utilization" as a bare percentage smuggles
in two choices: busy *doing what* (crafting? powered? merely occupied?)
and busy *out of what* (the whole window? the time the machine
existed?). FISL deliberately has no metric named "utilization": when the
course starts measuring busyness (Lab 4), every such number will name
its numerator states and its denominator explicitly.

For now, one honest preview from pure arithmetic: a non-constraint
machine in a line running at rate $m$ can be doing useful work at most
$m/\text{capacity}$ of the time. The *faster* a machine is relative to
the constraint, the *lazier* it must look. Hold that thought; it will
turn diagnosis upside down in Lab 4.

## Claims to carry into Lab 2

Lab 2 is a three-stage line — 37.5, 30, and 45 workpieces per minute —
with live diagnostics deliberately withheld. Commitments, in writing:

1. Measured throughput will be **30/min exactly** — the minimum, nothing
   blended.
2. The two reference interventions upgrade one machine each. The one
   that touches a non-constraint will change throughput by **exactly
   nothing**; the one that touches the constraint will move the line to
   the *new* minimum — compute it before running.
3. You can name the constraint from catalog arithmetic before the run
   starts, and the withheld diagnostics cannot stop you: the machine
   whose capacity equals the measured line rate is the constraint.

If claim 2's first half feels too strong — surely *some* improvement
leaks through? — good. That intuition is exactly what the lab exists to
correct, and in a deterministic world the correction is total.

## Further reading

- Hopp & Spearman, *Factory Physics* (3rd ed.), ch. 7 "Basic Factory
  Dynamics" — bottleneck rate and line parameters; ch. 18 "Capacity
  Management" for the decision-making layer this course only touches.
- E. M. Goldratt & J. Cox, *The Goal* (1984) — the constraint idea as
  narrative; the five focusing steps are Lab 2's debrief in novel form.
